A parallel historical reference

Ancient Western Asia
3200–500 BCE

From the Sumerian city-states to the early Persian Empire, alongside the Levant, Anatolia, the Zagros, Arabia, Elam, Afghanistan and Turkmenistan.

How to read this reference

The central idea is simultaneity: while a dynasty ruled at Ur or Babylon, neighboring societies had their own histories. A culture, a kingdom, a trading community and a province are not interchangeable categories.

Thirty-year indexing is not thirty-year precision. Middle Chronology for third/second-millennium Mesopotamia: Ur III 2112–2004; Hammurabi 1792–1750; Babylon I ends 1595. Alternative chronologies shift some dates by decades. Early archaeological boundaries can be uncertain by a century or more. These are regional historical reference cells, not territorial maps. A culture is not necessarily a kingdom; a dynasty’s lifespan is not uniform control of a whole region. Thirty-year intervals are an index, not an assertion of thirty-year precision. Unknown does not mean uninhabited. Names and date variants are normalized only where stated.
A Archaeological horizon; rulers mostly unknown
P Named polity/dynastic phase; boundaries still conventional
M Mixed / several polities / uneven imperial relations
U Political reconstruction especially uncertain

Bands run 3200→3170, 3170→3140, …, 530→500 BCE. Shared endpoints are plotting boundaries, not double-counted 31-year periods. Internal phase transitions remain visible. A separate endpoint snapshot represents 500 BCE.

Complete core sequences are explicitly labelled. Selected sequences have deliberate gaps. Undated names are not projected into specific 30-year bands. Ruler lists are neither exhaustive for every local polity nor proof of uninterrupted sovereignty.

Geographic key

CodeReference regionModern locationPrincipal sites / peoplesScope
SMSumer / BabyloniaSouthern and central IraqUruk; Ur; Eridu; Nippur; Kish; Lagash/Girsu; Umma; Isin; Larsa; Babylon; Sippar; Eshnunna/Diyala (separate neighboring kingdom)Several simultaneous city-states before and between territorial empires.
NMAssyria / Upper MesopotamiaNorthern Iraq; northeastern Syria; southeastern TurkeyAssur; Nineveh; Kalhu; Dur-Sharrukin; Nagar/Tell Brak; Urkesh; HarranAssyria and the Jazira are not always under one ruler.
SYInland SyriaWestern/central Syria and middle EuphratesEbla; Mari; Aleppo/Yamhad; Qatna; Emar; Carchemish; Hamath; DamascusIncludes competing Amorite, Hurrian and Aramean states; no single Syrian kingdom.
LCLevantine coastCoastal Syria and LebanonUgarit; Byblos; Arwad; Sidon; Tyre; AmurruCoastal cities often kept local dynasts under foreign overlords; Ugarit did not survive as an Iron Age kingdom.
SLSouthern LevantIsrael and Palestinian territoriesJerusalem; Samaria; Megiddo; Hazor; Gezer; Lachish; Ashkelon; Gaza; Ekron; Ashdod; GathIsrael, Judah, Philistine cities and Canaanite predecessors are distinct political histories.
TJTransjordanJordanRabbath-Ammon; Heshbon; Dibon; Bozrah; Edomite/Arabah copper districtsKingdoms of Ammon, Moab and Edom developed at different times; early dates are schematic.
WAWestern AnatoliaWestern TurkeyTroy; Beycesultan; Arzawa/Apasa; Seha River Land; Mira; Wilusa; Sardis; Greek coastal citiesTroy is an archaeological site with disputed links to Wilusa; Homeric kings are not dated here.
CACentral AnatoliaCentral and northern TurkeyHattusa; Kanesh/Kultepe; Kussara; Pala; Kaska regions; GordionHattian, Hittite, Luwian and other labels are not interchangeable.
SECilicia / southeastern AnatoliaSouthern and southeastern TurkeyKizzuwatna; Que; Hilakku; Tabal; Melid; Gurgum; Kummuh; Samal; CarchemishMountains, plains and Euphrates states had differing levels of imperial control.
EAEastern Anatolia / highlandsEastern Turkey and adjoining Armenian highlandsIsuwa; Hayasa-Azzi; Nairi; Lake Van; Tushpa; Erebuni; MusasirUrartian collapse is uncertain: late seventh/early sixth century, not a universally fixed year.
NZNorthern Zagros / UrmiaNortheastern Iraq and northwestern IranLullubum; Simurrum; Turukkean lands; Zamua; Mannea; Izirtu; Hasanlu; Zikirtu; AndiaAncient ethnic and geographic labels are not modern national boundaries.
CZCentral Zagros / MediaWestern and west-central IranLuristan; Godin; Bit-Hamban; Ellipi; Ecbatana/HamadanEarlier Luristan archaeological horizons cannot be assigned a continuous royal dynasty.
ELElam / SusianaKhuzestan and adjacent southwestern IranSusa; Awan (location uncertain); Haft Tepe/Kabnak; Chogha ZanbilElam also involved Anshan in Fars; Susiana was not always governed with the highlands.
FAFars / Anshan / PersisSouthwestern Iranian plateauTal-e Malyan/Anshan; Pasargadae; PersepolisPersia is not a synonym for all Iran or for earlier Elam.
EIEastern Iranian plateauKerman, central/eastern Iran and adjacent BaluchistanShahdad; Halil Rud/Jiroft; Tepe Yahya; Bampur; later Aria and DrangianaMarhashi is usually placed in southeastern Iran, but precise identification is disputed.
HEHelmand / southern AfghanistanSouthern Afghanistan and Iranian SistanMundigak; Shahr-i Sokhta; Arghandab; Kandahar/ArachosiaThe Helmand civilization crosses the modern Iran–Afghanistan border.
BABactria / northern AfghanistanNorthern Afghanistan and southern Uzbekistan/TajikistanBactra/Balkh; Dashly; Shortugai; Badakhshan lapis sourcesBMAC is an archaeological complex, not the name of a known unified kingdom.
TMSouthern Turkmenistan / MargianaKopet Dag foothills and Murghab oasis, TurkmenistanAltyn Depe; Namazga Depe; Anau; Gonur; Togolok; Yaz Tepe; MervKopet Dag sequences and Margiana sequences are related but not identical.
ANNorthwestern ArabiaNorthwestern Saudi Arabia and adjoining desertTayma; Dadan/al-Ula; Qurayyah; Khaybar; YathribOasis communities existed long before their royal names enter written evidence.
ACNorthern / central Arabian interiorSaudi interior and Syrian-Arabian desert marginsDumat al-Jandal/Adummatu; Qedarite and other tribal territoriesNot a continuous kingdom or a single ethnic bloc.
ADEastern Arabia / DilmunBahrain, eastern Saudi Arabia and Failaka/KuwaitTarut; Qalat al-Bahrain; FailakaThe center and extent of Dilmun changed; do not apply a fixed Bahrain-only boundary to 3200 BCE.
AMSoutheastern Arabia / MaganOman and United Arab EmiratesHafit; Umm an-Nar; Bat; Hili; Wadi Suq; later MakaMagan is conventionally linked to Oman/UAE; Maka’s exact borders are debated.
ASSouthwestern ArabiaYemen and adjoining southwestern Saudi ArabiaMarib/Saba; Sirwah; Jawf; Awsan; Qataban; HadramawtSaba, Awsan, Qataban, Hadramawt and Jawf states have separate histories. Early Minaean chronology is debated; no continuous pan-Arabian dynasty.
AFEastern Afghanistan / Hindu KushKabul region, Hindu Kush and Afghan/Pakistani borderlandsKapisa region; Kabul valley; Gandhara frontierGandhara extends into modern Pakistan; later Gandharan kingdoms must not be projected into 3200 BCE.
TWWestern / northern TurkmenistanCaspian littoral, Dehistan and lower Amu Darya fringeDehistan; Sumbar; lower Amu Darya/Khwarazm frontierTurkmenistan is modern; these zones were not one ancient territory.

Part two

Royal lines and known rulers

The transition from Ur III to the Isin–Larsa period and Babylon was not a neat relay: dynasties overlapped. The chart makes that overlap visible. Full names, dates and caveats follow.

369 registry entries do not mean 369 unique or equally secure monarchs. The registry includes selected local sequences, undated rulers, disputed successions and a few explanatory records. Complete core sequences are explicitly labelled.

Major events, wars and trade

Events and exchange networks are separate tables: tribute is not automatically commerce, and a military expedition does not necessarily imply permanent annexation.

Trade and exchange networks

The dates below are broad operating windows, not claims that every route ran unchanged throughout. This is not a reconstruction of a single Bronze Age “Silk Road.”

Window BCENetworkGoodsMechanism / settingCautionSources
3200→2900Southern Mesopotamia ↔ upper Euphrates / IranPottery, metals, stone, foodstuffs; administrative practicesInterconnected settlements and exchange corridorsUruk material culture outside Sumer is not automatic proof of conquest.S02 S08 S11 S87
3200→2000Badakhshan ↔ Iranian plateau ↔ Mesopotamia / LevantLapis lazuli and other prestige stonesMulti-stage overland exchange; exact itineraries usually inferredObjects can travel through many intermediaries; not direct royal control of mines.S27 S32 S69 S87
2600→1900Mesopotamia ↔ Dilmun ↔ Magan ↔ IndusCopper, timber, carnelian, shell, textiles and other goodsMaritime trade and Gulf intermediaries; Meluhha usually associated with Indus landsAncient names change scope; maritime connections do not define a single state.S14 S15 S28 S87
2500→2000Ebla / Mari ↔ Mesopotamia, Anatolia and coastTextiles, silver, timber and livestockPalace-managed exchanges and wider commerceArchive coverage is selective; not a full census of the economy.S55 S56 S77
2500→1700Helmand / BMAC ↔ Iran, Indus and steppe contactsLapis, carnelian, metals, crafted goodsOverlapping oasis and valley networksPolitical identities and exact routes uncertain; no named BMAC king list.S29 S32 S67 S69
2000→1750Ashur ↔ Kanesh and Anatolian townsTin and textiles outward; silver and gold in returnFamily firms, credit, donkey caravans and local trading quartersMerchant colonies are not an Assyrian territorial empire.S64
2000→1500Dilmun and changing Gulf routesCopper, dates, textiles and other goodsHarbor settlements and later Kassite-linked administrationChanging prosperity is not equivalent to total cessation of trade.S15 S28 S88
1500→1200Levant ↔ Cyprus, Aegean, Egypt and AnatoliaCopper, tin, glass, ivory, timber and luxury goodsMerchant shipping, court gifts and redistributionA wreck’s cargo is a sample, not a complete ancient trade balance.S06 S09 S72
1200→900Post-palatial Mediterranean / inland networksMetals, timber, ceramics and agricultural productsReorganized local and maritime exchangeNetworks change unevenly; commerce does not disappear everywhere.S07 S10 S24
1000→500Phoenician ports ↔ MediterraneanTimber, metalwork, textiles, manufactured goodsIndependent city networks, settlements and maritime enterprisePhoenicia is not one centrally ruled empire.S24 S65
1000→500South Arabia ↔ north Arabian oases ↔ LevantFrankincense, myrrh and other caravan goodsOasis agriculture, caravan transport, tolls and diplomacyStarting dates are broad; no universal camel revolution on a single year.S16 S49 S50 S70 S71
900→612Assyrian core ↔ provincial and tributary regionsMetals, textiles, horses, livestock and manpowerCommerce alongside tribute, taxation, deportation and forced laborTribute and plunder are not the same as voluntary trade.S23 S34 S49
750→500Anatolia / Iran ↔ eastern oasis and steppe zonesHorses, metals and crafted goodsRegional exchanges alongside conflict and migrationAvoid calling all early Eurasian contacts a fully formed Silk Road.S07 S13 S19 S30
550→500Achaemenid provinces ↔ imperial centersAgricultural produce, silver, textiles, livestock and specialized goodsRoads, royal communication, tax systems and local merchant networksAdministrative integration does not abolish regional institutions or frontier autonomy.S25 S30 S59
